name: Time, Speed & Distance
intro: **Before computing, name the quantity being held constant.** Distance constant ⟹ invert the speed ratio. Time constant ⟹ distances are proportional to speeds. Naming it first kills the average-speed and ratio-inversion errors in one move.
Convert units before anything else: km/h → m/s is ×5/18. Mixing units mid-solution is silent — the arithmetic looks fine and the answer is off by 3.6.

qs.q: Walking at 5/6 of his usual speed, a man reaches office 8 minutes late. Find his usual time (in minutes).
qs.h: §1 — speed ratio 5 : 6 inverts to a time ratio of 6 : 5. The 8 minutes is one part.
qs.s: Time ratio (new : usual) = 6 : 5. The difference of 1 part is 8 minutes ⟹ usual time = 5 parts = 40 minutes.

qs.q: Increasing his speed by 20%, a man reaches 12 minutes early. His usual time is
qs.h: §1 — a 20% increase is a speed ratio of 6 : 5 (new : usual), so the time ratio is 5 : 6.
qs.s: Time ratio (new : usual) = 5 : 6 ⟹ difference of 1 part = 12 min ⟹ usual = 6 parts = 72 min.

qs.q: A boy walking at 4 km/h reaches school 5 minutes late; walking at 5 km/h he is 10 minutes early. Find the distance to school (in km).
qs.h: §1 — the two journeys differ by 15 minutes in total. Set up d/4 − d/5 = 15/60.

qs.q: A train travelling at 3/5 of its usual speed is 40 minutes late. Its usual time for the journey is
qs.h: §1 — here the difference is 2 parts, not 1. Divide before multiplying.
qs.s: Time ratio (new : usual) = 5 : 3 ⟹ difference of 2 parts = 40 min ⟹ 1 part = 20 ⟹ usual = 3 parts = 60 min.

qs.q: If a man reduces his speed by 25%, he takes 20 minutes more. Find his usual time (in minutes).
qs.h: §1 — a 25% reduction is a speed ratio of 3 : 4, so the time ratio is 4 : 3.
qs.s: Time ratio (new : usual) = 4 : 3 ⟹ difference of 1 part = 20 min ⟹ usual = 3 parts = 60 minutes.

qs.q: Two men cover the same distance, one at 30 km/h and the other at 40 km/h. The slower one takes 2 hours longer. The distance is
qs.h: §1 — d/30 − d/40 = 2. Or: time ratio 4 : 3, difference 1 part = 2 hours.
qs.s: d/30 − d/40 = 2 ⟹ d/120 = 2 ⟹ d = 240 km. Check: 8 hours and 6 hours ✓

qs.q: A car goes from A to B at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole trip (in km/h).
qs.h: §3 — equal distances, so the harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b). The arithmetic mean 50 is the decoy.

qs.q: A man drives at 30 km/h for 2 hours and then at 50 km/h for 2 hours. His average speed is
qs.h: §3 — equal times, not equal distances. Here the ordinary average is correct.
qs.s: Equal times ⟹ average = (30 + 50)/2 = 40 km/h. (37.5 is the harmonic mean — the equal-distance answer, planted as a decoy.)

qs.q: A man covers three equal distances at 10, 20 and 60 km/h. Find his average speed (in km/h).
qs.h: §3 — three equal distances: 3abc/(ab + bc + ca). Or assume the LCM 60 for each leg.

qs.q: A person travels 150 km in 5 hours, partly at 20 km/h and partly at 40 km/h. The distance covered at 40 km/h is
qs.h: §3b, algebraic constraint — let x be the distance at 20 km/h, then answer the question actually asked.
qs.s: x/20 + (150 − x)/40 = 5 ⟹ 2x + 150 − x = 200 ⟹ x = 50 km at 20 km/h ⟹ at 40 km/h he covers 100 km. (50 km is the other leg — the trap.)

qs.q: A man travels the first half of a 60 km journey at 20 km/h and the second half at 30 km/h. Find the total time taken (in hours).
qs.h: §3b — tabulate each leg and sum the times. Do not average the speeds first.
qs.s: 30/20 + 30/30 = 1.5 + 1 = 2.5 hours. (Average speed = 60/2.5 = 24 km/h, which is 2ab/(a+b) ✓)

qs.q: A journey of 90 km is done in three equal legs at 30, 45 and 90 km/h. The average speed is
qs.h: §3 — three equal distances again. Assume 90 km total ⟹ each leg 30 km.
qs.s: Times: 1 + 2/3 + 1/3 = 2 hours for 90 km ⟹ 45 km/h. (The arithmetic mean of 30, 45, 90 is 55 — the decoy.)

qs.q: A thief 300 m ahead runs at 9 km/h; a policeman chases at 12 km/h. After how many seconds is the thief caught?
qs.h: §4 — same direction, so relative speed is the difference. Convert to m/s before dividing.
qs.s: Relative speed = 3 km/h = 3 × 5/18 = 5/6 m/s ⟹ time = 300 ÷ 5/6 = 360 seconds (6 minutes).

qs.q: Two cyclists 120 km apart ride toward each other at 15 km/h and 25 km/h. They meet after
qs.h: §4 — opposite directions, so the speeds add.
qs.s: Relative speed = 40 km/h ⟹ time = 120/40 = 3 hours.

qs.q: Two cars start from the same point in the same direction at 50 km/h and 65 km/h. After how many hours are they 45 km apart?
qs.h: §4 — the gap grows at the relative speed.
qs.s: Gap grows at 15 km/h ⟹ 45/15 = 3 hours.

qs.q: A car overtakes a bus that is 3 km ahead, in 20 minutes. If the bus travels at 45 km/h, the car's speed is
qs.h: §4 — find the relative speed first, then add the bus's speed. 20 minutes is 1/3 hour.
qs.s: Relative speed = 3 ÷ (1/3) = 9 km/h ⟹ car = 45 + 9 = 54 km/h.

qs.q: A and B start walking toward each other from points 84 km apart at 4 km/h and 3 km/h. A dog runs continuously between them at 10 km/h. Find the total distance the dog covers (in km).
qs.h: §4 — you don't need the dog's path at all, only how long it runs. Find the meeting time first.
qs.s: They meet after 84/(4 + 3) = 12 hours ⟹ the dog runs for 12 hours at 10 km/h = 120 km.

qs.q: A train 240 m long crosses a pole in 12 seconds. Find its speed in km/h.
qs.h: §5 — crossing a pole means covering exactly the train's own length. Convert with 18/5.

qs.q: A train 180 m long crosses a platform 270 m long in 25 seconds. Its speed is
qs.h: §5 — crossing a platform means train length + platform length.
qs.s: Distance = 450 m in 25 s = 18 m/s = 64.8 km/h. (Using only the 180 m gives 25.92 km/h — the classic slip.)

qs.q: Two trains of lengths 150 m and 250 m travel in opposite directions at 45 km/h and 27 km/h. Find the time (in seconds) to cross each other.
qs.h: §5 — opposite directions, so speeds add; both lengths count.
qs.s: Relative speed = 72 km/h = 20 m/s; distance = 400 m ⟹ time = 20 seconds.

qs.q: A 250 m train running at 90 km/h overtakes a cyclist riding at 18 km/h in the same direction. The time taken is
qs.h: §5 — the cyclist has no length, so only the train's length is covered, at the relative speed.
qs.s: Relative speed = 72 km/h = 20 m/s ⟹ time = 250/20 = 12.5 seconds.

qs.q: Two trains running in the same direction at 72 km/h and 54 km/h cross each other in 40 seconds. If the faster train is 120 m long, find the length of the slower train (in metres).
qs.h: §5 — same direction, so the relative speed is the difference; the distance covered is the sum of the lengths.
qs.s: Relative speed = 18 km/h = 5 m/s ⟹ combined length = 5 × 40 = 200 m ⟹ slower train = 200 − 120 = 80 m.

qs.q: A train crosses a pole in 15 seconds and a 300 m platform in 30 seconds. The length of the train is
qs.h: §5 — the speed is the same in both cases. Equate L/15 and (L + 300)/30.

qs.q: A boat covers 36 km downstream in 3 hours and the same distance upstream in 6 hours. Find the speed of the stream (in km/h).
qs.h: §6 — get D and U first, then s = (D − U)/2.

qs.q: A man rows at 8 km/h in still water; the stream flows at 2 km/h. He rows to a place 24 km away and returns. The total time is
qs.h: §6 — D = 10, U = 6. Add the two leg times; never average the speeds.

qs.q: A boat's downstream speed is 15 km/h and its upstream speed is 9 km/h. Find its speed in still water (in km/h).
qs.h: §6 — b = (D + U)/2. One of the two formulas worth memorising.

qs.q: A man takes 3 times as long to row upstream as downstream. The ratio of his speed in still water to the speed of the stream is
qs.h: §6 — time ratio m : n gives b : s = (m + n) : (m − n).
qs.s: m : n = 3 : 1 ⟹ b : s = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1. (Answering 3 : 1 is using the time ratio directly — the trap.)

qs.q: A boat covers 30 km upstream and 44 km downstream in 10 hours; and 40 km upstream and 55 km downstream in 13 hours. Find the speed of the boat in still water (in km/h).
qs.h: §6 — substitute u = 1/U and d = 1/D to turn this into a linear pair, then solve.
qs.s: 30u + 44d = 10 and 40u + 55d = 13. Multiply the first by 4/3 and subtract: 11/(3D) = 1/3 ⟹ D = 11. Then 30/U = 6 ⟹ U = 5. b = (11 + 5)/2 = 8 km/h (s = 3).

qs.q: A boat's speed in still water is 10 km/h and the stream flows at 2 km/h. Its average speed for a round trip is
qs.h: §6 — the round-trip average is (b² − s²)/b, and it is always strictly less than b.
qs.s: (100 − 4)/10 = 9.6 km/h. It must be below 10 because more time is spent going upstream.

qs.q: Two runners on a 400 m circular track run at 8 m/s and 12 m/s in opposite directions from the same point. After how many seconds do they first meet?
qs.h: §9 step 4 — opposite directions, so together they cover one full lap.

qs.q: Two runners on a circular track run at 8 m/s and 12 m/s in the same direction from the same point. The number of distinct meeting points on the track is
qs.h: §9 step 1 — reduce the ratio first. Same direction gives a − b.
qs.s: 8 : 12 = 2 : 3 (coprime) ⟹ meeting points = 3 − 2 = 1, so they only ever meet at the start. (Not reducing gives 12 − 8 = 4 — the trap.)

qs.q: Two runners on a 600 m track run at 5 m/s and 10 m/s in the same direction from the same point. After how many seconds do they meet at the starting point for the first time?
qs.h: §9 — "at the starting point" is the LCM of the lap times, a completely different formula from "anywhere".
qs.s: Lap times = 120 s and 60 s ⟹ LCM = 120 seconds. (Meeting anywhere would be 600/5 = 120 s too, because the reduced ratio 1 : 2 gives just one meeting point.)

qs.q: On a 900 m circular track, A runs at 15 m/s and B at 25 m/s in opposite directions from the same point. The number of distinct meeting points is
qs.h: §9 — reduce 15 : 25 first, then add.
qs.s: 15 : 25 = 3 : 5 ⟹ 3 + 5 = 8 meeting points, spaced 112.5 m apart. (Forgetting to reduce gives 40 — an option, deliberately.)

qs.q: Three runners start together from the same point on a 300 m circular track at 3, 5 and 7 m/s, all in the same direction. After how many seconds are all three together again?
qs.h: §9, three runners — compute the pairwise meeting times, then take their LCM.
qs.s: Pairwise gaps 2, 2 and 4 m/s ⟹ meeting times 150 s, 150 s, 75 s ⟹ LCM = 150 seconds. Check: distances 450, 750, 1050 all reduce to the 150 m mark ✓

qs.q: On a 400 m track, A and B start together in the same direction at 6 m/s and 10 m/s. B first gains a full lap on A after
qs.h: §9 — gaining a lap means the relative distance covered equals the circumference.

qs.q: Two runners start from opposite ends of a 400 m stretch at 6 m/s and 10 m/s and keep bouncing back and forth. After how many seconds do they meet for the 4th time?
qs.h: §7 — the nth meeting needs a combined distance of (2n − 1)D.
qs.s: Combined distance = (2×4 − 1)(400) = 2800 m at 16 m/s ⟹ 175 seconds.

qs.q: A and B start toward each other from P and Q. After meeting, A takes 9 hours to reach Q and B takes 16 hours to reach P. They met after
qs.h: §8 — t = √(t₁ t₂). Note that 25 (the sum) is planted as an option.

qs.q: A and B move toward each other from P and Q. After they meet, A takes 4 hours to reach Q and B takes 25 hours to reach P. Find the ratio of A's speed to B's speed, as a decimal.
qs.h: §8 — Speed A : Speed B = √t₂ : √t₁. The inversion is the whole question.
qs.s: A : B = √25 : √4 = 5 : 2 = 2.5. A has the shorter remaining time, so A must be the faster runner — a free sanity check.

qs.q: Two people start from opposite ends of a 240 m track at 4 m/s and 8 m/s and keep bouncing. Their 2nd meeting occurs after
qs.h: §7 — 2nd meeting means a combined distance of 3D, not 2D.
qs.s: 3 × 240 = 720 m at 12 m/s ⟹ 60 seconds. (Using 2D gives 40 s — an option, deliberately.)

qs.q: A and B start toward each other at the same time from P and Q, 210 km apart. After meeting, A takes 4 hours to reach Q. If A's speed is 30 km/h, find B's speed (in km/h).
qs.h: §8 — the leg A still has to cover after meeting is exactly the leg B had already covered. Find it, then find the pre-meeting time.
qs.s: After the meeting A covers 4 × 30 = 120 km, so B had covered 120 km before the meeting and A had covered 90 km. Pre-meeting time = 90/30 = 3 hours ⟹ B's speed = 120/3 = 40 km/h. Check: 30 + 40 = 70 and 210/70 = 3 ✓

qs.q: A cyclist rides north at 9 km/h and another rides east at 12 km/h from the same point at the same time. How far apart are they (in km) after 3 hours?
qs.h: §3c — perpendicular motion, so use Pythagoras on the positions, not relative speed. Look for the 3-4-5 triple.

qs.q: Two ships leave the same port at the same time, one sailing due south at 24 km/h and the other due west at 7 km/h. After 2 hours they are
qs.h: §3c — 7-24-25 is a Pythagorean triple. Option (a) is the sum of the speeds ×1 — the additive error.

qs.q: A is at the origin moving north at 12 km/h. B starts 15 km east of A and moves north at 2 km/h. Find the distance between them (in km) after 2 hours.
qs.h: §3c, different start points — write both positions, take the coordinate differences, then Pythagoras.
qs.s: After 2 h: A = (0, 24), B = (15, 4). Separation = √(15² + 20²) = 25 km.

qs.q: Ship P is at (0, 0) sailing east at 10 km/h. Ship Q is at (0, 40) sailing south at 30 km/h. Their separation is least at
qs.h: §3c, closest approach — write D² (never D) as a quadratic in t and use t = −b/2a.

qs.q: Two men start from the same point along roads inclined at 60° to each other, walking at 5 km/h and 8 km/h. Find the distance between them (in km) after 1 hour.
qs.h: §3c, non-perpendicular bearings — the cosine rule, with cos 60° = ½.
qs.s: D² = 25 + 64 − 2(5)(8)(½) = 89 − 40 = 49 ⟹ D = 7 km. (Using Pythagoras here would give √89 ≈ 9.43 — wrong, because the angle isn't 90°.)

qs.q: Walking at 6/7 of his usual speed, a man is 12 minutes late. His usual time is
qs.h: Invert the ratio; the 12 minutes is one part.
qs.s: Time ratio 7 : 6 ⟹ 1 part = 12 min ⟹ usual = 6 parts = 72 min. (84 = 7 parts is the new time — the trap.)

qs.q: A train 300 m long crosses a bridge 500 m long in 40 seconds. Find its speed in km/h.
qs.h: Both lengths count; convert at the end.

qs.q: A man rows 15 km downstream in 1 hour 15 minutes and 15 km upstream in 3 hours. The speed of the stream is
qs.h: Get D and U, then (D − U)/2.

qs.q: Two trains 130 m and 110 m long move toward each other at 60 km/h and 84 km/h. Find the time (in seconds) to cross each other.
qs.h: Opposite directions; both lengths.
qs.s: Relative speed = 144 km/h = 40 m/s; distance = 240 m ⟹ 6 seconds.

qs.q: A car covers the first 60 km at 40 km/h and the next 60 km at 60 km/h. Its average speed is
qs.h: Equal distances — harmonic mean.
qs.s: 2(40)(60)/100 = 48 km/h. (50 is the arithmetic mean — the standing decoy.)

qs.q: A and B start toward each other from towns 120 km apart at 20 km/h and 30 km/h. How far from A's town (in km) do they meet?
qs.h: Meeting time first, then A's own distance.
qs.s: Time = 120/50 = 2.4 h ⟹ A covers 20 × 2.4 = 48 km. (72 km is the distance from B's town.)

qs.q: On a 500 m circular track, A and B run in opposite directions at 20 m/s and 30 m/s from the same point. The number of distinct meeting points is
qs.h: Reduce the ratio before adding.
qs.s: 20 : 30 = 2 : 3 ⟹ 5 meeting points. (Unreduced gives 50 — an option.)

qs.q: A man walking at 5 km/h reaches his office 6 minutes late; at 6 km/h he is 2 minutes early. Find the distance to his office (in km).
qs.h: The total time gap is 8 minutes, not 6.

qs.q: After they meet, A takes 25 hours to complete his journey and B takes 36 hours. The ratio of A's speed to B's speed is
qs.h: The square roots, inverted.
qs.s: A : B = √36 : √25 = 6 : 5. A finishes sooner, so A is faster — the check that catches the inversion.

qs.q: Two runners start from opposite ends of a 500 m stretch at 4 m/s and 6 m/s and keep bouncing between the ends. Find the time (in seconds) of their 5th meeting.
qs.h: (2n − 1)D with n = 5.
qs.s: Combined distance = 9 × 500 = 4500 m at 10 m/s ⟹ 450 seconds.

audit: using the speed ratio as the time ratio, or reading the wrong part as the answer (§1)
A3, M8
treating a "late by x, early by y" pair as a gap of x instead of x + y
using the arithmetic mean where equal distances demand the harmonic mean (§3)
B2
using the harmonic mean where the times, not the distances, are equal
B4
solving for the wrong leg and reporting it
mixing km/h with metres instead of converting by 5/18 first (§2)
C5
trying to sum the dog's zig-zag legs instead of using the total running time
D2, D6
forgetting the platform length, or the train's own length
D4, D5
using the wrong relative speed for the stated direction (§5)
E2, E6
averaging the two leg speeds for a round trip instead of (b² − s²)/b (§6)
E4
using the time ratio directly as b : s instead of (m + n) : (m − n)
not reducing the speed ratio to lowest terms before counting meeting points (§9)
F3
using the "meet anywhere" formula where "meet at the start" needs the LCM of lap times
using nD instead of (2n − 1)D for the nth bounce meeting (§7)
inverting the √ trick — Speed A : Speed B = √t₂ : √t₁, not √t₁ : √t₂ (§8)
adding distances instead of applying Pythagoras to perpendicular motion (§3c)
H4
minimising D instead of D², which turns a clean quadratic into a mess
H5
using Pythagoras where the angle between the paths is not 90° — use the cosine rule
